scenario_M_KDS_3_S1_single_bump_empirica.event: Vuex action dispatches POST with fresh X-Idempotency-Key (UUID v4 per call)
scenario_M_KDS_3_S1_single_bump_empirica.code_path: kds.js:3-9 kdsStatusPayload(order, status) = { id, status, expected_status: order.status }. resources/js/store/modules/kitchenDisplaySystemOrder.js:37-52 dispatches axios.post('admin/kds-order/change-status/' + payload.id, payload, { headers: buildIdempotencyHeaders(payload) }). helpers/idempotencyHeaders.js:27-33 generates crypto.randomUUID() unless payload.idempotency_key is explicit (it is NOT for KDS — kdsStatusPayload omits it). NET: every bump click ships a fresh X-Idempotency-Key — the middleware will NEVER collapse two KDS bumps to a Phase-1 replay; protection is solely on the expected_status optimistic-lock + lockForUpdate serialisation. This is INTENTIONAL because the KDS path uses optimistic concurrency (cheaper than payload-hash idempotency).

routes/api.php:1129-1131 Route::post('/change-status/{order}', [KitchenDisplaySystemController::class, 'changeStatus'])->middleware(['idempotency', 'throttle:kds-bump'])->name('change-status'). idempotency middleware (IdempotencyKeyMiddleware.php:39-157) — fresh key always passes Phase-1 lookup miss, acquires Phase-2 slot, executes Phase-3, caches 2xx response for 86400s (config('idempotency.ttl_seconds')). scenario_M_KDS_3_S4_two_chefs_same_order.scenario: 2 chefs (multi-station kitchen) bump the SAME PREPARING order simultaneously
steps: Chef A device: order card shows PREPARING. Posts { status: PREPARED, expected_status: PREPARING } with its own X-Idempotency-Key UUID-A.
Chef B device: same order card shows PREPARING (cross-screen state not yet propagated by broadcast). Posts identical body with its own X-Idempotency-Key UUID-B.
Idempotency middleware: KEYS DIFFER (different UUIDs) → both pass through Phase-1 lookup miss. Both Phase-2 acquire succeeds for distinct scoped keys.

Controller routes both into KitchenDisplaySystemOrderService::changeStatus. Both DB::transactions begin. One acquires the row lockForUpdate; the other BLOCKS on MySQL InnoDB row lock until the first commits.
Winner: $fromLocked=PREPARING (DB) = expectedFrom=PREPARING (request) → canTransition OK → save PREPARED → commit. 202 response.

Loser (after first tx commits, second tx unblocks): re-reads via lockForUpdate → $fromLocked=PREPARED (post-winner commit) ≠ expectedFrom=PREPARING → writes [KDS_409] → abort(409). HTTP 409 to chef B.

Empirical bench: transitions_rows = 1 (not 2) — clean audit trail. Audit_logs chain UNTOUCHED (KDS path does not call AuditLogService::write — verified by grep on KitchenDisplaySystemOrderService.php + OrderStateMachine.php — no AuditLogService import or call site).

honest_caveats: Tinker bench reported the 409 path with `Plain Exception caught -> code=0 msg=...` instead of HttpException. The HTTP-level sentinel `KdsExpectedStatusConflictSentinelTest` is the authoritative evidence for HTTP 409 status (assertStatus(409) PASS in 532.91ms at HEAD). The tinker output is a class-binding artifact of interactive REPL eval — does NOT reflect real HTTP routing behavior.

Empirical S2 multi-bump runs SEQUENTIALLY in tinker (single-process, not concurrent threads). True concurrent N-threads racing on the same row would require forked PHP / external HTTP load. The `KdsChangeStatusConcurrencyTest` sentinel exercises the lockForUpdate via the simulated stale-fetch pattern (Order::query()->update between fetch and service call) which provably hits the same row-lock surface.

S4 2-chef race in tinker simulates by cloning the route-bound model — the actual concurrent HTTP path would have two separate request stacks competing on the lockForUpdate. The defense surface is identical because both paths route through the same service entry point, and the lockForUpdate is the only serialisation primitive.
